content.title: NUTRITION FACTS THAT SOUND LIKE INTERNET MYTHS BUT ARE 100% REAL
facts: **Cashews** are never sold in their shell to consumers — the shell contains a resin so caustic it's related to poison ivy, and it has to be steamed off industrially before the nut is safe to touch.
**Nutmeg** contains a natural compound called myristicin that, in large enough doses (several whole nutmegs), can cause hallucinations — it's technically a mild, dangerous psychoactive spice.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange — the orange variety was selectively bred in the Netherlands in the 1600s, partly as a tribute to the House of Orange.
**Chewing gum** has been found still intact after thousands of years — archaeologists discovered a piece of birch-bark tar gum in Sweden with visible human tooth marks from the Stone Age.
**Rhubarb** stalks are a common dessert food, but its leaves contain enough oxalic acid to be genuinely toxic if eaten in quantity — the plant is edible and poisonous at the same time.
**Almonds** are technically not nuts at all — they're the seed found inside the pit of a fruit closely related to peaches and cherries.
**Apples** float in water because roughly 25% of their volume is air pockets between the flesh cells — a fact you can test in your own sink right now.
**Bananas** are mildly radioactive because of their naturally high potassium content, enough that scientists actually use the 'banana equivalent dose' as a joking unit to explain radiation exposure.

content.caption:
A few of these deserve a closer look. Take cashews — the shell contains urushiol, the exact same irritant found in poison ivy, which is why raw-in-shell cashews basically don't exist on store shelves anywhere in the world. Nutmeg is wilder than it sounds too: myristicin is metabolized by your liver into a compound structurally similar to certain stimulants, which is why 'nutmeg tripping' is a real (and genuinely risky) thing teenagers have tried. And rhubarb's leaves are so high in oxalic acid that they can bind with calcium in your blood and strain your kidneys — yet the stalks right next to them are perfectly fine in a pie. Everyone's tolerance and body chemistry differs, so this is general food trivia, not medical advice.
